title: Mango Markets: the $114M oracle squeeze
lossUsd: ~$114M drained (~$117M across 14 tokens by some counts)
status: Convicted April 2024; conviction overturned on May 23, 2025 (judge found insufficient evidence of false representation to a permissionless protocol)
tldr: In under an hour, a trader used two anonymous accounts and roughly $10M of his own capital to pump the price of a thinly traded governance token, MNGO, on the exchanges that fed Mango Markets' oracle. The protocol trusted that fake price, valued his unrealized perp profits at hundreds of millions, and let him borrow out almost every real asset in the vault. There was no code bug. Every transaction was valid. He just lied to the price feed - and the risk engine believed it.

background.label: What it is
background.text: Mango Markets was a trading platform built on Solana smart contracts - think of a crypto exchange with no company in the middle. There was no website holding your coins; the rules were code, and anyone could use it.

background.label: What it does
background.text: On Mango you could do three things from one account: buy and sell tokens (spot), take leveraged bets that a token would go up or down (perpetual futures), and lend or borrow against your balances to earn or pay interest.

background.label: How it works
background.text: The core idea is 'cross-margin.' Instead of separate wallets for each trade, one account holds your tokens, your open positions and your loans together, and a single number - your health - decides how much you are allowed to borrow. To compute that number, the platform constantly needs to know what everything is worth.

background.label: Where prices come from
background.text: Mango did not decide prices itself. It used an oracle that read a token's price off several exchanges and averaged them. If those exchanges had thin trading, the price was easy to nudge - and because borrowing power depended on that price, nudging a price meant nudging how much anyone could borrow. That is the door the attacker walked through.

mechanism:
Mango Markets was a cross-margined trading platform: one account could hold spot balances, perp positions and debt, and a single 'health' number decided how much it could borrow. The price of MNGO - used to value MNGO perp positions - came from an oracle that averaged MNGO's price across spot venues (Mango itself, plus external exchanges). Those venues had almost no MNGO liquidity.

That combination is the whole exploit:

1. **Fake the price.** Buy a few million dollars of MNGO on those thin venues. With a shallow order book, a modest buy walks the price up violently - from ~$0.038 to ~$0.91 - and the oracle faithfully reports the new number.
2. **Fake the profit.** One account was long 483M MNGO-perps; the other short. The inflated oracle marked the long side's *unrealized* profit at hundreds of millions.
3. **Borrow against the fiction.** The risk engine accepted that unrealized profit as collateral, so the short account could borrow and withdraw ~$116M of real BTC, USDT, SOL and mSOL.
4. **Pull the rug back down.** Once he stopped buying, MNGO collapsed to its old price. The collateral was worth a fraction of the debt, leaving the protocol with ~$115M of bad debt - and real users holding worthless claims.

timeline.event: The attacker moves ~$14M USDC from a Circle account through an exchange account, sending ~$5.5M and ~$5M to two fresh Solana wallets (court filings call them 'Solana Wallet-1' and 'Wallet-2').
Both wallets fund two separate Mango Markets accounts with ~$5M USDC each, giving him two identities on the same protocol.

Wallet A posts an offer to sell 483M MNGO-perpetual futures at $0.038. Wallet B buys all of it. The two accounts are on opposite sides of one trade - a wash trade that manufactures a huge position without a real counterparty.
He spends a few million dollars buying MNGO on the thin spot venues that feed the oracle across Mango, AscendEX and FTX. The oracle price rockets.
MNGO spikes as much as ~24x, peaking near $0.91. The oracle reports the artificial high, inflating the collateral value of the long account.
Wallet B borrows and withdraws ~$116M of real assets against the fake collateral - the single largest withdrawal is ~$54M USDC, followed by ~$25M mSOL. Mango is drained of nearly all user funds.
He stops buying. MNGO collapses back toward its pre-attack price, leaving ~$115M of bad debt stranded in the protocol.
An anonymous DAO proposal appears demanding ~$70M as a 'bug bounty' and asking the protocol not to pursue criminal charges. It is voted on using the MNGO acquired in the attack.
Avraham Eisenberg publicly identifies himself, calling the exploit 'a highly profitable trading strategy' and arguing 'all of our actions were legal.'
~$67M is returned to Mango after a DAO vote; ~$47M is kept.
Eisenberg is arrested in Puerto Rico; the DOJ, CFTC and SEC all bring charges.
A Manhattan jury finds Eisenberg guilty of fraud and market manipulation.

U.S. District Judge Arun Subramanian overturns the fraud and market-manipulation convictions, ruling prosecutors failed to prove Eisenberg made false representations to a permissionless, smart-contract-run protocol. Eisenberg is separately still serving a four-year sentence from an unrelated 2024 guilty plea.

actors.label: MNGO
actors.role: The asset used to fake the collateral
actors.note: The governance token whose thin, easily-moved price the oracle trusted. Verify the mint address character-for-character - fake MNGO clones exist.

actors.label: Mango Markets
actors.note: A cross-margined spot + perpetuals + lending platform on Solana. Its oracle and risk engine - not its code - were the weak points.

actors.label: Solana Wallet-1 / Mango Account-1
actors.role: Funder and long side of the wash trade
actors.note: Received ~$5.5M USDC from an exchange account the attacker controlled. Opened an anonymous Mango account and took the 483M MNGO-perp long.

actors.label: Solana Wallet-2 / Mango Account-2
actors.role: Short side, then the withdrawal account
actors.note: Received ~$5M USDC. Took the matching short, then borrowed and withdrew the ~$116M against the inflated long.

actors.label: Attacker-controlled exchange account
actors.note: Registered in a different person's name with a foreign address, funded from a Circle account. The upstream common source is a key linkage clue for investigators.

transactions.label: Wash trade setup
transactions.description: Wallet A sells 483M MNGO-perps at $0.038; Wallet B buys all of it. No real counterparty - the same person on both sides.

transactions.label: Oracle pump
transactions.description: A few million dollars of MNGO buys across thin spot venues walk the oracle price up ~24x to nearly $0.91.

transactions.label: The squeeze
transactions.description: Wallet B borrows and withdraws ~$116M of real assets (~$54M USDC and ~$25M mSOL among the largest) against the fake collateral.

researchMethod.step: Turn the headline into three questions
researchMethod.detail: The headline is a starting point, not an answer. 'Mango was hacked for $114M' tells you almost nothing. Your very first move is always the same: pin down WHAT moved, WHEN it moved, and WHICH address touched it. Convert the story into questions you can actually answer on a block explorer.
researchMethod.doThis: Open the protocol's official statement (their X/Twitter post or blog) next to a block explorer. Write down three facts: the exact date and time in UTC, the asset that left, and the chain it was on.
researchMethod.lookFor: Vague wording. If the team says 'funds were drained' but never says how, that gap is exactly where your investigation starts.
researchMethod.example: Mango, October 11 2022, Solana. The twist: the attacker did not steal one token - he walked out with ~$116M of real BTC, USDT, SOL and mSOL. So the real question became: 'how were those real assets unlocked?'

researchMethod.detail: Money never vanishes - it moves. Ignore the narrative and find the account that GAINED and the account that LOST. Spotting that transfer is the single most useful skill in on-chain analysis.
researchMethod.doThis: Open the abused token on the explorer and filter its transfers/holders to the attack day, sorted by size. Then open the victim protocol's own main account and read its recent token transfers in and out.
researchMethod.lookFor: A brand-new address - created hours earlier, almost no history - receiving an enormous amount in a single transaction. That is almost always the attacker.
researchMethod.example: On Mango's side you can see the attacker's account borrow and withdraw ~$116M in minutes, led by ~$54M USDC and ~$25M mSOL. No wallet received that much from Mango before - that spike is the anomaly.

researchMethod.step: Walk the money backwards to the funder
researchMethod.detail: Every attacker's wallet has a birthday. Follow its very first transaction upstream and you usually find an exchange, a bridge, or a single source that also funded their other wallets.
researchMethod.doThis: Open the suspect wallet, go to its transaction/transfer history, and scroll all the way to the OLDEST entries. Note who sent the first funds and exactly when.
researchMethod.lookFor: Two or more wallets that look unrelated but were seeded by the same funder. Shared funding is how investigators prove 'one person, many accounts'.
researchMethod.example: Mango's two 'anonymous' accounts were both funded from ONE exchange account the attacker controlled - court filings (SDNY) trace ~$5.5M and ~$5M from that single source into two fresh Solana wallets minutes apart.

researchMethod.detail: Now the fun part: figure out the 'how'. Read the suspicious transaction step by step and match each move to what the protocol was supposed to allow.
researchMethod.doThis: Open the biggest transaction on the explorer and expand it fully. On Solana, read the instruction list top to bottom (including inner instructions). On EVM, expand the decoded logs and call trace.
researchMethod.lookFor: A sequence that only makes sense if someone is lying to the system: an oracle update right before a borrow, two accounts trading with each other, a fake number accepted as collateral.
researchMethod.example: Mango: the tell is a wash trade - two fresh accounts opened 483M MNGO-perps against each other at $0.038. Then a few million dollars of MNGO buys spiked the oracle to ~$0.91, and the 'profitable' side borrowed against that fake number.

researchMethod.step: Prove the exit and cross-check the numbers
researchMethod.detail: A case only becomes 'proven' when the money leaving matches independent sources. Never trust a single report - triangulate until the picture is consistent.
researchMethod.doThis: Trace where the stolen value went (the outflows), total it yourself, then compare against neutral trackers and security-firm post-mortems.
researchMethod.lookFor: Number alignment - and disagreement. When sources differ it usually reveals exactly which assets were counted, and how. Mango is reported as both ~$114M and ~$117.8M for that reason.
researchMethod.example: Mango: your on-chain withdrawals line up with Elliptic's ~$117.8M across 14 tokens. The SEC, CFTC and DOJ filings then turn the raw on-chain picture into a named, charged, legally-documented case.

redFlags: The MNGO oracle was a volume-weighted price over markets with almost no liquidity - a few million dollars could move it ~24x.
The risk engine treated *unrealized* perpetual profits as borrowable collateral, so paper gains became real withdrawals.
Two anonymous accounts traded a 483M-token position against each other (a wash trade) - a classic manipulation footprint.
The position size dwarfed the protocol's real liquidity, meaning any honest valuation would have rejected it.

sources.label: Elliptic — Mango exploit analysis ($117.8M across 14 tokens)
